items.object: Interpretability research on language models
items.answer: Interpretability research is trying to understand how the models do what they do at all. If you're familiar with the field, you're like, "Yes, this makes sense." items.question: How do you understand Claude 3.5 Haiku’s ability to plan ahead when writing rhyming poetry?
items.object: Claude 3.5 Haiku’s planning when writing rhyming poetry
items.answer:
You can imagine it would get to the end of the rhyme and then it'd be like, "Oh, now I have to rhyme with orange." And it's like, well, turns out actually that's a hard rhyme. Also, I didn't think about it. But still, you can imagine, well, maybe if you have enough data, it just kind of always picks sentences that make sense, and it gets to the rhyme and there's some murky thing.

But it turns out that what we found when we looked at it was that when Claude 3.5 Haiku is given a rhyming couplet—the example we used in the paper is, "He saw a carrot and had to grab it"—the model then completes that with, "His hunger was like a starving rabbit." It rhymes using rabbit, which is fine. It turns out that when it processes "grab it," and then comma, and then new line, and it's about to write the second line, before it writes the first word of the second line, there are features, representations in the model's circuits for the word rabbit.

It's already decided, in a way, if you want to say decided, that it's going to end with rabbit. Then it uses those representations not just to choose rabbit at the end. They're also causally involved; they help guide the choice of all of the words before leading to rabbit. We know this because we see it in the circuit, but also because we want to validate this outside of our methods. We perform a bunch of tests where we delete rabbit and add a random word—in the paper we use green—and then the model rewrites the sentence completely. I think the sentence it lands on is something like, "The farmer's field was verdant green," or something. So it completely changes its sentence so that it can end with its plan. That example of pretty complex, longer-horizon behavior was definitely one that stuck with me as something that you might not expect if you were just like, well, they're just autocomplete on steroids, predicting the next token. items.question: How do you understand the interpretability challenge posed by transformers compared with decision trees?
items.object: The interpretability of decision trees versus transformers
items.answer:
In past jobs doing machine learning, I've used models that weren't transformers, models like decision trees. Decision trees are commonly used in fintech and fraud prevention and stuff like that. They have this really nice property that they're exactly what they sound like. They're this tree of decisions. Once you've trained your model, you can look at it and say, "The reason that the model said we should block this transaction is because the amount was over $10,000 and it was going to a bank account in the Cayman Islands or something." And you're like, yeah, that makes sense. Whereas if the individual branches made less sense, you'd be a little more suspicious. That's a really nice property of these simpler models. Turns out transformers are not at all like that, the complete opposite.

The way that they work is they have these giant vectors of numbers, hundreds or thousands of numbers, that represent each word or each token, and then those get processed by a series of, basically, often millions or billions of computations. At the end, the model predicts a word, and what happens in between, if you look at all of these numbers, is completely unclear. You can go in your Jupyter notebook and look at the numbers and say, "Yes, when Claude was writing poetry, this is the sequence of a billion numbers or whatever that was in its activations," but so what? It's maybe similar to looking at a tangled mess of cables or circuitry inside a computer. You could look at what lights up, but you need to somehow map your observation to what the model is actually thinking about. That's the nature of the problem.

items.question: How do you think about dictionary learning as a way to understand what a language model is representing?
items.object: Dictionary learning for interpreting language model representations
items.answer:
The idea is, can you take this dense mess of numbers inside the model when it's processing one word or one sentence, and decompose it into a bunch of unique concepts? If the model is processing the prompt, "I'm taking my car over the Golden Gate Bridge," you might expect that you see this mass of numbers, but in it there's going to be a concept for the Golden Gate Bridge, a concept for car, and a concept for a fun weekend with friends or something. The goal of dictionary learning is, can you decompose representations into a sparse version that's understandable?

We do that in an unsupervised manner, basically. You train a completely other model that's going to be your dictionary, that's going to decode the innards of your base model. Then on a given prompt you can look and say, "Look, Claude was thinking about this or thinking about that." That was the paper prior to these most recent ones, and we found a bunch of interesting things there. We found very nuanced representations. There's representations for people being sycophantic, meaning praising you even when they don't mean it. There's representations for typos and bugs in code. There's a bunch of different representations inside the model that are fascinating.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between word embeddings and the more nuanced concepts represented inside a language model?
items.object: The relationship between word embeddings and concepts represented inside language models
items.answer:
It's definitely related. The models themselves take in embeddings for their words. Then they process these embeddings and output different vectors, essentially. An example we have in the paper is facts: "Michael Jordan plays the sport of," and basketball is the completion that the model successfully gets to. How does it know this? One thing models do is take the embedding for Jordan, which is just a token they've learned, and various pieces of the model read this embedding and will write, for example, basketball, Space Jam, or the Chicago Bulls.

These embeddings are your starting point, but then you have a lot more nuance about various aspects of decomposing or combining them. If you have Michael Jordan and LeBron, maybe you're going to have some parts of the model that combine those and start to have features for discussing who's the greatest basketball player of all time. Debates about greatness is probably a feature there.

The way I think about it is that the nuances of concepts that can be represented in the model are a combinatorial explosion on top of your embeddings. You have your base embeddings, and then you can combine them in various ways. You might have an embedding for street, and an embedding for Main Street, First Street, Second Street, Third Street, but then you're also going to have a direction in the model that's Main Street in Texas, maybe, or Main Street in Arizona. You can combine them in arbitrary ways. What we're trying to understand are these more complex and nuanced representations inside the model after it's consumed embeddings and before it's output an actual prediction.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between a language model’s initial token embeddings and the shared representations it uses across languages?
items.object: Shared representations across languages inside language models
items.answer:
The comparison we make in the biology paper on this is, if you do, I think it's the opposite of large is small, which is the French version, and you do different languages, what you find is initially there are different embeddings for those because they're different tokens. Then, as the signal progresses through the model, the features, these representations, start being shared. There's a shared representation of something that is big, a shared representation of something that is the opposite across all languages.

All of the embeddings for big and large and all of the other languages share at least one facet, which is that they're about something that's big. They have many other facets they don't share. One of them starts with B, the other starts with L. They have different numbers of letters, whatever. There's a bunch of ways in which they're different. They're in different languages, but they share that.

The model, in processing these different languages, extracts the shared representation and then does its computation. It's like, there's largest, there's opposite, so I have to say something small, and then goes back to the language that it was asked in. In the paper, we're like, well, if it's truly a shared set of representations, surely it means you can mess with them and plug one for the other, or use the same flip large to small in the shared space, and it'll do the same thing for all languages. Surely it does, meaning we don't need to find a different concept of opposite in French and Chinese and English. We found the concept of opposite for the model here, and we turn it on; it works for all languages. Again, it's something more nuanced than the original embedding. It's extracted some aspect that is shared, and it is useful for it to generalize when it's learning across languages. That's also an important implication here: that allows you to learn something in French text and then be able to apply that same circuit that you learned in texts of other languages.

items.question: How do you understand sparse coding as a way to make a language model's internal representations comprehensible?
items.object: Sparse coding and dictionary learning for interpreting language-model representations
items.answer:
The idea is actually similar both for this new paper and for the dictionary learning papers. It's the same approach, basically. You have, say, in the middle of the model, this very dense vector of numbers. In that vector, you're pretty sure are all these representations: the representation of large, the representation of opposite. But all you see is this dense vector of numbers, and what you want is to know, actually the model is thinking a little about concept A, a little about concept B, and a little about concept C. This is just a method to get at that. The way we get at it is to learn a separate model that will take this incomprehensible mass, this dense vector, and learn essentially—you do a matrix multiply—to a much larger space. Then you force that space to be very sparse.

If you have, let's say, a hundred neurons somewhere in the middle of your model, you have a hundred numbers that are always active and very hard to comprehend. You blow it up to a thousand numbers, and you have a constraint that says, basically, in your loss, you penalize every time one of those numbers is not zero. The model is going to have to be very parsimonious in allocating these features. It's not going to be able to turn many of them on. That's where the sparse comes from. Then you have to make sure you're actually capturing as much as you can. You try to reconstruct the original thing from that code. You're learning a sparse code and also making sure your sparse code is enough to capture as much of the original thing as possible. That's basically the gist of dictionary learning. You're training with this mix of sparsity and reconstruction error: how well can you reconstruct after you've blown it up and put it back together?

That is what gives you these features, which we call monosemantic, meaning they kind of represent only one thing.

items.question: Why do you see moving from sparse autoencoders to transcoders as useful for understanding a model's computation?
items.object: Transcoders versus sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting model computation
items.answer: There's a space of tradeoffs here. Going from SAEs, which are just doing it on the neurons, to transcoders is nice because that allows you to understand computation rather than just representation. Once we've replaced these parts of the model, we can directly connect features to features. You can say, this feature at this layer writes in that direction, because now you've replaced a part of the model. The feature is just a computation: the computation writes that direction, and this other feature reads in this direction. They don't talk to each other at all, but those features go in the same direction, and so they talk to one another.

items.question: How do you assess the prospect of replacing a language model with an equally capable, fully interpretable alternative?
items.object: Replacing a language model with an equally capable, fully interpretable alternative
items.answer:
Ignoring money or physics for a second, which is always fun, with unlimited money and infinite data and stuff like that, you could totally imagine replacing the whole model with this interpretable alternative and running it instead. Then we get a free lunch, basically, where we have something as good as the base model and we can understand it.

In actuality, it's more like up-distilling than distilling. Because all of the layers are way wider, even if I could give you this perfect model, it'd be really expensive to serve, because it's a way bigger object than the base model. There's also a question of training costs. In our biggest Haiku 3.5 runs, there were 30 million features, and those are pretty big runs.

If you're doing the per-layer thing, then a feature is an encoder and decoder, so two vectors. But if you're doing this cross-layer thing, the way it works is a feature is one encoder and then n layers of decoders. So it's actually quite expensive. But that is still worth it because you need fewer features, because you're deleting a bunch of redundant features. A feature is on the order of maybe close to what a neuron in an MLP would cost you. Thirty million of them is a lot, but think about how many independent concepts the model knows. We call it the dark matter problem in the paper.

There's a problem: how many features would we need so that we captured everything that Claude knows? Currently, using our methods, that's probably on the order of billions, maybe. That's quite infeasible with today's tech. It would cost way too much to train; it'd be completely impossible to even study it. It'd be this giant monster. In order to capture everything the model is doing, and so to both explain it fully but also be able to reconstruct it accurately, we need so many features that right now this is still basically an unsolved problem. One thing that's relatively clear, and that we talk about in the paper, is we're going to need to think of smart ways to get features more efficiently, or get features more efficiently only in a domain that we care about. Maybe we don't care to explain how Claude does everything. Maybe we only care to explain how Claude does math or how Claude does PI or something. That buys us a lot. But there are methods you could imagine using to be more efficient with your features that we discuss a little bit.

That's the dream. Right now the realistic state we're in is we can explain some of what the model is doing some of the time. The first step after that is, can we keep increasing the proportion of times that we understand what's going on? I don't know if we'll ever get to the dream of replacing the model with the interpretable model, but even if we just manage to understand a lot more, we'll get a lot of value here.

items.question: Why do you use features rather than individual neurons to understand what a language model is doing?
items.object: Polysemantic neurons and monosemantic features in language models
items.answer:
One thing you might think is, why do we need to do this at all? The model already has neurons. We could just use them and do our graphs based on that. It turns out that if you just look at the neurons and try to understand them the way that we try to understand features, which is run it on a bunch of text and see what makes it light up, and see if when you look at that pattern it's obvious what it does—so for features like the Golden Gate Bridge feature, if you run it on a bunch of text and highlight the parts where it lights up, it's like you're literally just highlighting the text "Golden Gate Bridge" in a bunch of text, and everything else is very clear. Most neurons are not like that at all. Most neurons you look at and you're like, it seems to fire on sevens sometimes, but only if there was Russian language before and also German cookbooks. Or even that is kind of understandable. It mostly just looks kind of random.

That's because each neuron isn't a meaningful unit for the model. The model uses a bunch of neurons in parallel and stores representations over all of them. Those neurons are what we call polysemantic. They just don't have a single meaning. Whereas the features are monosemantic. You can say, this is the Michael Jordan feature. If it has a very high activation, that means the model is thinking a lot about Michael Jordan. If it doesn't, it's not.

items.question: How do you understand superposition as an explanation for the dense representations inside a language model?
items.object: Superposition in language model representations
items.answer: The idea of superposition, then, is how do you reconcile this idea that there are features that are very meaningful and very sparse with the fact that if you look inside the model, it's a very dense thing where, in the residual stream of the model, which is where information is processed, everything is on all the time. There's no sparsity. The hypothesis is essentially superposition. What's happening is the model is storing many more features than it has dimensions in superposition and squishing them tightly, such that when you look at it, it's just this mess. But actually, each feature is smeared across many dimensions, and our work is to decode that smearing into these abstract monosemantic things, basically untangle the superposition to get the monosemantic representations. That's the name of the game here.

items.question: Why do you see attention as the biggest limitation of your circuit-tracing method?
items.object: Attention as a limitation of the circuit-tracing method
items.answer:
Attention is the biggest one by far. There are many other limitations, don't get me wrong. We touched on one, which was this dark matter: if you extrapolate how many features we have and how many features we need, we're just not going to get there. We need to find a way to do it more efficiently. Attention is a huge one because there are many things the model does that are almost entirely done via attention. A common example is induction, when the model looks back at previous instances of the word it's processing, looks at what was said after that word, and then says the same thing. That's interesting, but actually pretty well understood.

There's a lot of stuff we don't understand, or at least that's harder to understand. A better example is multiple-choice questions, where the model has to answer B. The way it says it's answer B is that there's an attention head that looks at B and then writes it at the end. If you use our method, that's basically all you see. You're like, "Great. The complete story of what happened on this prompt is that Claude somehow knew that the answer was B, and then an attention head moved it there." But of course, the interesting question is, why did this attention head look at B? There's some computation that happens in the model that tells it the correct answer was B, and then it looks at B and copies it. Currently, we completely sidestep that.

We explain part of attention, or at least we explain how attention moves the information from MLPs, but we don't explain why attention patterns were the way they were. A huge part of how the model processes information is how it decided to attend from X to Y, something that we completely miss. Obviously, it's one of the main limitations and aspects we're interested in working on, and hearing from other groups working on it. Solving that is by far the most exciting thing on my list in terms of next work. I don't think it would be easy, to be clear, but I think it's doable.

items.question: Why do you think attention mechanisms in language models are difficult to interpret?
items.object: Interpreting attention mechanisms in language models
items.answer:
I think there are a few reasons why attention is hard, but none of them are fundamental. You totally could train some sparse replacements for parts of attention. Attention is just different in a few ways.

One way is that the other aspects we replace are, maybe univariate is the wrong word, but you take the state of the model, apply your MLP, and write the result. You can replace that; it's a very clean computation. Attention patterns specifically are the combination of what's happening at all of the key positions and all of the query positions, and the interactions between both of those. So now you have something that's quadratic, basically, and you have to find a way to get around that. There are proposed approaches, and I think some of them are likely to work, or at least I hope they are. A lot of the limitation is computational bounds, for the same reason attention is hard to scale for context windows and stuff like that.

Another one is nonlinearity over attention. It's not just you're doing a k-cube, and then you're also doing your nonlinearity, which means you have to think carefully about your decomposition efforts. In our graphs, because of our replacement, we've managed to make everything linear, so you can say this feature affects that one in that way. Here it's like, this key affects relationships—but actually, what really matters is that that one was much stronger, and so you didn't really have an effect at all. You are getting squished by the nonlinearity.

items.question: How do you see interpretability contributing to safety audits before a model is released?
items.object: Interpretability as a model safety auditing tool
items.answer: Interp is part of our safety portfolio here. One example, again, in the biology is there was this auditing game that was run recently where a model was acting strangely. It turns out it had been trained to act strangely, but in a way that's not obvious. My hope, and I think the team's hope, is that tools like interp can help with things like that. In the case of that game, interp was helpful. You could also figure out what's wrong with the model without interp. For complex reward-hacking behavior or behavior where we might not notice the model is acting strangely, and be concerned about the implications of that, like what does it mean that the model is acting strangely in these contexts, being able to explain the mechanisms through which it's acting that way feels really valuable as an auditing step in any model-auditing pipeline before you decide to release it and the extent to which you feel comfortable releasing it.
